nary_nodes.label: Soyuz launch
evidence: Physician-astronaut Anil Menon, a former flight surgeon with NASA and then SpaceX who rejoined NASA as an astronaut along with his wife Anna, rocketed into space Tuesday with two Russian cosmonauts for an eight-month stay aboard the International Space Station.
Soyuz MS-29/75S commander Pyotr Dubrov, flanked on his left by cosmonaut Anna Kikina and on the right by Menon, blasted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan at 10:47 a.m. EDT.
nary_nodes.type_definition: An event where a rocket or spacecraft is launched into space.
nary_nodes.type_justification: No schema.org event matches a space launch; minting with Event as parent.

nary_nodes.label: Soyuz docking
evidence: Eight minutes and 46 seconds later, the Soyuz was released to fly on its own, catching up with the station after just two orbits and moving in for docking at 1:52 p.m.
But the ship flew itself in for a picture-perfect docking at Russia's Earth-facing Prichal module as the two spacecraft sailed 260 miles above the Mediterranean Sea.

nary_nodes.label: Welcome aboard ceremony
evidence: After post-docking leak checks were complete, the new crew members were welcomed aboard the ISS by Soyuz MS-28/74S commander Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Andrey Mikaev and NASA astronaut Chris Williams, along with crew 12 commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.
They gathered in the Russian Zvezda module for a brief welcome aboard ceremony with flight controllers, managers and friends back on Earth.

evidence: Physician-astronaut Anil Menon, a former flight surgeon with NASA and then SpaceX who rejoined NASA as an astronaut along with his wife Anna, rocketed into space Tuesday with two Russian cosmonauts for an eight-month stay aboard the International Space Station.
The fresh Soyuz crew is expected to remain aboard the station for about 260 days, returning to Earth next April.

nary_nodes.label: Menon's surprise
evidence: "In terms of me and Anna, I would say there was a zero percent chance we thought this would happen, but it does go to show that if you keep working at something, you should never count yourself out," Anil Menon said.

nary_nodes.label: Menon on paths
evidence: "It also goes to show that if you're interested in being a part of NASA, going to space, there's a lot of different ways this could work out. There isn't a set course. Sometimes... if you work hard and consistently over time, the results can be completely shocking. We've been absolutely shocked by this."

nary_nodes.label: Isaacman congratulations
evidence: "Congratulations, crew, on a impressive three-hour (rendezvous)," he radioed from Baikonur. "And to my friend Anil, how are you enjoying space flight?"

nary_nodes.label: Menon's reply
evidence: "Hello, it's great to hear from you," Menon replied. "An incredibly fast ride! I'm feeling great."

nary_nodes.label: Isaacman pride
evidence: "I know you all have a lot of work to do right now, so just passing on to you (that) all your friends here, your family, your nation are proud of you," Isaacman said. "Godspeed and God bless on the expedition ahead."

nary_nodes.label: Menon thanks
evidence: "Thank you very much for those kind words," Menon said. "The station is a sight to behold and a monument to all the hard work we are able to do together and what we're able to achieve when we do it.

nary_nodes.label: Dubrov welcome
evidence: "It's a great tradition when the arriving crew is welcomed by the smiley faces of our crewmates," Dubrov said through an interpreter. "We passed a lot of time together during our training, and now we are here all together on the station. And also, those traditional hugs. It's so amazing, it's very warm and comes from the heart."

nary_nodes.label: Menon on stress
evidence: "When we talk about what it was like for her to launch and me to be on the ground, I think that was the harder job, and I found it really stressful," he said. "I was worried about her and the kids, and there were certain challenges related to that.

nary_nodes.label: Menon on understanding
evidence: "I'm able to share that perspective with her, so I'm like, hey, heads up, like it's going to be a lot easier for me to do this launch."

For her part, he added, "she's got insight into what that's like (to fly in space) and what the launch might be like, and how to make it meaningful.... We've talked a lot about that. I think, like, either side of this, my side and her side, hopefully we're better off, and we understand each other a bit better."

nary_nodes.label: Menon on Dubrov
evidence: Menon said he was lucky to be flying with space veterans like Dubrov and Kikina. He described his Soyuz commander as "kind of on the quieter side, really intellectual, really sharp."

"He speaks incredibly good English, and he's into Rubik's cubes and esoteric science fiction. He's read the Foundation series (by) Isaac Asimov, and Murderbot before the TV shows made those things popular. We really hit it off, because I love science fiction, too, and that's super cool."

nary_nodes.label: Menon on Kikina
evidence: As for Kikina, who first flew to space aboard a Crew Dragon in 2022, Menon described her as "100 percent full on energy, and really adds a lot to our team because me and Pyotr are a bit more quiet, and so it's really cool to have her just like keep the engine running and moving us along.

"And she's an athlete, like a rafter boater, she was on the Russian version of American Gladiator -- it's called Titan -- and won that easily. And so it's a cool crew, an interesting, fun crew to be a part of as well. They've also flown to space, so I got a lot to learn and pick up from them, and it's a good spot to be in."
